nameStory: This plant earns its 'evening primrose' name from its fascinating nighttime blooming habit - the flowers typically open in the evening and stay open through the night, then close by morning. The 'northern' part of its name reflects its preference for cooler climates compared to its southern cousins. Despite the name, it's not actually related to true primroses at all!
description: Northern evening primrose is a tall, upright wildflower that can reach 2-5 feet in height. It produces bright yellow, four-petaled flowers that bloom along a central spike from summer into early fall. The plant has a somewhat weedy appearance with lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately up the stem. As a biennial, it spends its first year as a low rosette of leaves, then shoots up to bloom in its second year.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with exactly four petals arranged in a cross pattern, about 1/2 to 3/4 inch across - noticeably smaller than common evening primrose. Each flower has a long, thin tube at the base and opens in the evening with a sweet, lemony fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves with slightly toothed edges that feel somewhat rough and hairy to the touch. They're arranged alternately up the stem and have prominent white veins running through the green surface.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a tall, unbranched or slightly branched spike reaching 2-5 feet high. First-year plants form a flat rosette of leaves close to the ground, while second-year plants bolt upward to flower.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops narrow, four-sided seed capsules that split open when ripe to release numerous small, dark seeds. The capsules feel dry and papery when mature and make a subtle rattling sound when shaken.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Sturdy, upright stem that's often reddish-tinged and covered with fine hairs. The stem feels rough to the touch and may have a slightly sticky quality from tiny glandular hairs.

habitat: Northern evening primrose thrives in disturbed soils and open areas throughout New England, including roadsides, old fields, railroad tracks, and waste places. It prefers well-drained, sandy or gravelly soils and full sun exposure. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy species like goldenrod, asters, and other evening primroses in areas that have been cleared or disturbed.

seasonality.spring: First-year plants appear as small rosettes of hairy leaves close to the ground. Second-year plants begin sending up their flowering stalks in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with yellow flowers opening each evening and closing by morning. The sweet fragrance is strongest in the evening hours when flowers first open.
seasonality.fall: Late flowers may continue blooming into early fall, while seed capsules mature and split open to release seeds. The plant begins to die back after setting seed.
seasonality.winter: Dead stalks with empty seed capsules may persist through winter, creating rattling sounds in the wind. First-year rosettes may survive under snow cover.

funFact: The flowers of northern evening primrose literally open before your eyes in the evening - if you watch closely around dusk, you can actually see the petals unfurl in a matter of minutes, sometimes with an audible 'pop' sound as the flower opens!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common evening primrose, but northern evening primrose has noticeably smaller flowers (less than 3/4 inch vs. 1-2 inches across). Remember: 'northern' means 'smaller' when it comes to evening primrose flowers. The fragrance is also typically sweeter and more lemony in northern evening primrose.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'primrose,' evening primroses are completely unrelated to true primroses (Primula species). The name confusion arose because early botanists noticed both groups had similar-looking yellow flowers, but evening primroses belong to an entirely different plant family.
compareHints: Among New England's evening primroses, northern evening primrose stands out for its smaller flower size compared to common evening primrose and Large-flowered evening-primrose. Unlike the low-growing small sundrops, northern evening primrose grows tall and upright. It's also more consistently biennial than some of its relatives, always forming that distinctive first-year rosette before blooming.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common evening-primrose is the tallest and most robust of New England's evening-primroses, with the largest flowers.
Small sundrops differs from its evening primrose relatives by staying low and sprawling rather than growing tall and upright like common evening primrose.
Meadow evening primrose is much less common than its cousin common evening primrose, which grows much taller (3-6 feet) and has larger flowers that open in the evening.
Unlike the bold, large yellow flowers of common evening-primrose that can be 2 inches across, clockweed has tiny, delicate white or pink flowers only half an inch wide.
Unlike its yellow-flowered cousin common evening-primrose which grows tall and upright, pinkladies stays low and spreads horizontally.
Unlike its evening primrose cousins that typically have four-petaled yellow flowers opening at dusk, biennial beeblossom stands out with its pink flowers and incredibly tall, airy growth habit.
Unlike the tall, upright common evening primrose with its simple oval leaves, cutleaf evening primrose stays low to the ground with deeply divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Large-flowered evening primrose stands out from other Oenothera species primarily due to its impressive flower size - much larger than common evening primrose or the various sundrops species.
Among the many evening primroses in New England, red-stalked evening primrose stands out primarily for its reddish stem coloration, while most relatives like common evening primrose have green stems.
Unlike the common evening primrose which typically grows 3-5 feet tall, tall evening primrose can reach 6 feet, making it the giant of the genus.
Bigfruit evening primrose stands out dramatically from its New England relatives like common evening primrose due to its sprawling, ground-hugging growth habit rather than upright stems.
Yellow sundrops differ from common evening-primrose by blooming during the day rather than evening and having distinctive blue-green waxy leaves instead of plain green ones.
Among the evening-primroses in New England, Nodding Evening-Primrose is unique for its drooping flower buds - all other species have upright, erect buds.
